title: Bottle with Snake

altText: A ceramic bottle about twenty-two centimeters tall with a snake as part of its design.

context: A ceramic bottle with a snake, made by Moche artists on the coast of Peru between the 2nd and 5th centuries. It stands about 22 centimeters high. Moche potters often shaped plants, animals, and people into vessels.

descriptions.k: This clay bottle has a snake on it. A snake has a long, bendy body. Moche artists in Peru made this bottle long ago. It is about as tall as a water bottle. Can you follow the snake with your eyes?
descriptions.g12: Moche artists in Peru made this clay bottle with a snake on it. A snake has a long body that bends and curves. The bottle is about as tall as a water bottle. Trace the snake's path with your eyes. Where does it begin and end?
descriptions.g35: This bottle was made by Moche artists on the coast of Peru between the 2nd and 5th centuries. A snake is part of its design. The bottle is about 22 centimeters tall and made of ceramic. Look at how the snake's long body fits onto a rounded bottle. Why might a potter choose an animal with such a flowing shape?
descriptions.g68: Moche potters of Peru's coast often turned animals and plants into ceramic vessels, and this bottle, made between the 2nd and 5th centuries, features a snake. A snake's long, curving body is a good subject for clay because it can wind around a form. The record does not explain what the snake meant, and scholars are cautious about assigning single meanings to Moche images, so close description of the shapes comes first.
descriptions.g910: This Moche bottle, from the 2nd to 5th century, uses the long, curving body of a snake as a sculptural and decorative element on a ceramic vessel. Moche potters worked with modeled forms and surface finish to turn familiar animals into designs that suit a container. The record does not tell us what the snake meant or how the bottle was used, so interpretation should begin with careful observation of how line and volume work together.
descriptions.g1112: Made between the 2nd and 5th centuries, this Moche bottle with a snake belongs to a ceramic tradition in which animals frequently appear. The snake's winding body offers a natural line that animates a rounded vessel. Interpretations of Moche animal imagery range from observation of the natural world to symbolic readings, but without written Moche sources and without more context in the record, such readings remain hypotheses. The object invites analysis of how form, line, and function interact in sculptural ceramics.

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Title, classification (Ceramics-Containers), medium, and tag (Snakes) read from the museum record; the record does not flag the object as sacred or restricted and indicates no human remains, nudity, or weapons. A snake is a possible concern for some young students, so the text frames it neutrally and as a sculptural form.

teacherNote.context: The Moche lived on the coast of Peru in the early centuries CE and are known for modeled and painted ceramics. The record gives the subject as a snake and does not explain its meaning or use.
directions: Have students trace the snake's path in the air and describe the curve using line vocabulary.
Ask students to model a clay animal and attach it to a small cup.
Discuss the difference between describing what we see and guessing what it means.
